extracted.intended_audience: administrative analysts, procedure planners, and managers in government agencies and large organizations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing and planning administrative procedure and organization, including classification of functions, line vs. staff distinctions, and methods for studying and improving administrative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good procedure (business circulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good procedure is that which allows business to circulate smoothly and rapidly, and with the fewest interruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The flow of business is inherent in administration, arising from division of work and the need to relate each task to the next; its channels are determined by organization structure and habitual or planned patterns of procedure. A stoppage at any point will prevent other organs from functioning and may paralyze larger parts of the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific approach: base study on observed facts and be systematic
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid becoming a branch of political theology, it must stick closely to observed facts, and be systematic in its analysis of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study of administration should be as exact and scientific as possible, drawing on the 'scientific management' tradition while recognizing the limits of applying techniques developed for machine operations to administrative 'brainwork.' Concepts used should be grounded in reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize variability and discretionary nature of administrative work
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of administrative work is its variability; no two problems are the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike manual or routine clerical work, administration often requires discretionary decisions in professional fields (law, economics, sociology, medicine). Methods that work for repetitive industrial tasks may not apply; analysts must account for non-routine, imaginative, and personality-dependent work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage creative ability and initiative; avoid oppressive rules
rubrics_metrics.description: We want to encourage creative ability and initiative in the individual worker, therefore we must avoid oppressive rules and regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the same time the work of hundreds must be coordinated; good administration requires satisfying both the individual's need for freedom in work and the social need for regimentation. Procedures should be introduced so as to hurt people's feelings as little as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative management should produce consistent written procedure based on objective analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The visible result of administrative management consists for the most part of written procedure — plans of organization, regulations, and instructions for routing business and doing specific jobs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such procedure is often codified (e.g., manuals issued by Federal agencies and large companies) and should be consistent and based on objective analysis of administrative problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management planning must be based on facts and rigorous analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Planning is only possible when we have facts... The more elaborate the work being planned, the more detailed and accurate the data must be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts should be drawn from the problem itself, the organization, or relevant experience; analyzed, classified, expressed in comparable terms, and measured where possible. If quantitative exactness is impossible, be rigorous in qualitative analysis and avoid guesswork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of administrative analysis (three kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three kinds of facts ... There are thus three methods of administrative analysis: by function, by units of organization, and by administrative sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given an actual problem it may be possible to proceed in all three ways at once since the phenomena are different aspects of the same subject. Each method is explained separately, but may be combined in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define functions, sub-functions, and duties via classification
rubrics_metrics.description: A function is generally defined as a sphere of activity dealing with definitely limited subject matter, and having both a definite purpose and at least a moderately specialized technique. Within each function there are sub-functions — limited and more specialized branches — and within these are individual duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification is a fundamental phase of analysis. It is the systematic observation of similarities and relationships and serves as the basis for referring particulars to the general in scientific method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify functions into line and staff
rubrics_metrics.description: The first classification of an organization's functions is into two groups: line and staff functions. The line functions represent the purposes of administration; the staff functions embody administrative processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The difference varies by organization; what is a purpose in one may be a process in another. Staff units (accounting, personnel, purchasing) serve line units; they are as much operating agencies as line divisions though their activity is defined in terms of process rather than purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide line vs. staff by dominant technique relation
rubrics_metrics.description: A pragmatic basis for dividing work between line and staff units is whether the technique dominant in the situation is most closely related to the line or to the staff activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in purchasing, general market knowledge (a staff technique) may be dominant; for specialized scientific apparatus buying, close consultation with the user (line knowledge) may be necessary. Some activities (informational work, research) may be inseparable from line operations at times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification should not follow titles or existing org structure blindly
rubrics_metrics.description: The classification should not be too greatly influenced by the titles of functions ... Nor should classification necessarily follow the organization structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles like 'administrative audit' or 'liaison' may mean anything; classifiers must probe to find the real function. Classifications should guide efficient grouping rather than crystallize existing arrangements. Budgetary and file classifications often require adaptation before use for administrative analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: File classification must be systematic and reflect true functional framework
rubrics_metrics.description: A classification for use only in finding filed papers may be mnemonic, but one intended for general use in management must be systematic and reflect the true framework of functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compile file classification on the basis of data supplied by filing rooms and principals, under direction of those who understand the internal development of fields of work; consult officials and the Principal in Charge of Simplification and the Chief Clerk where advisable; sanction by top administrator to ensure acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involve officials and obtain top-level sanction for classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The administrative analyst in charge of making a classification should consult extensively with the officials in charge of each function, with similar officials in other organizations, and with outsiders versed in the subject matter. Finally the classification should be sanctioned by the top administrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consultation and sanction ensures the classification reflects true work, will be accepted as a basis for planning, and will serve management and reporting needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use functional classifications to support budgeting and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional classifications were developed for the use of administrative officials within departments and for setting up appropriation bills and accounts; since 1910 there has been a tendency toward setting up appropriations by functions and sub-functions rather than by objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such classifications serve municipal accounting, budget making, reporting, cost accounting, administrative control, and the compilation of financial statistics; they often reflect departmental breakdowns but may include functions distributed among departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis by function — Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Purpose: What is the direct activity (purpose of administration)? How does the administrative function facilitate the accomplishment of the direct work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin surveying a main function and work down to sub-functions and duties; at each level gather enough information to give a comprehensive picture of the activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis by function — Necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessity: Could the administrative activity in question be eliminated or curtailed? How essential is it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the activity is essential or redundant; consider whether elimination or curtailment is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis by function — Co-ordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-ordination: Are the direct operations and the administrative work consistent within themselves and with each other? Do they conflict in any way with other functions or with the major objectives of the organization?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for conflicts and consistency across functions and alignment with organizational objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis by function — Method
rubrics_metrics.description: Method: What operations are involved in the direct work? Specifically, how are these operations supervised?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail the operations that make up the function and describe supervisory arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis by function — Assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment: What unit or units carry on the function? What are the channels of supervision? How is the work divided — by sub-function, or by area of operation, or both? Are two or more units, which could be combined, doing the same or similar work? Is any work being done twice?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify units responsible, supervision channels, division of work, duplication, and opportunities to combine units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis by function — Work Load
rubrics_metrics.description: Work Load: How much working time, and of what type and grade of employees, is required? What is the unit of output? How many such units are produced?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify time, employee grades, output units, and production quantities where possible to inform staffing and resource decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis by function — Accomplishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Accomplishment: Does the function, as carried on and administered, serve its purpose? What improvements are needed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate effectiveness and identify needed improvements to better serve the function's purpose.
